text: Newsletters, websites and ads across competitors and industries are converging on the same Claude-aesthetic, the same tone of voice and the same way of articulating ideas . Most notably missing are the idiosyncratic markers of a human author; LLMs have processed them out to create a generic bleh , with one company’s output increasingly indistinguishable from another. johan michalove Oct 11, 2026 Share An AI-generated sign of a spa sign. Source. We might not know where we’ll be in 50 years, but if we were to look back at today half a century from now, would we know what we’ve lost? A lot of nostalgia, even future nostalgia, rides on subjectivities that have ceased to be possible. We might not talk about it as the structure of feeling that we are mourning, to borrow a term from Raymond Williams, but isn’t this exactly what we come to feel through nostalgia: the places we can’t go to (shuttered), the music we can’t reproduce (unobtainable), the way we didn’t know what tragedies were to occur (impossible). There’s a certain genre of urbanist who mourns the pre-automotive city. They talk about how cities used to be walkable before we started planning them for cars, and particularly in the US, made automobiles necessities. I wonder if there’s a similar thing happening with cognitive prosthetics and AI: we’re starting to build professions, knowledge work, and consumer products that can no longer be performed without AI as some kind of middleware. Fast forward 50 years, and it’s feasible that AI is so integrated, so inescapable, so infrastructural that we’ll have nostalgia for the pre-AI subjectivity. Inevitably, we won’t be able to recall exactly what the pre-AI world felt like, only the outward expressions of it. Already I’m seeing how real-world slop promises there’s no going back. Bodegas across NYC are increasingly plastered with exceptionally unappetizing AI-generated food illustrations. This is the death knell for a certain kind of vernacular food drawing style that now would be a signal of taste, not economy, to maintain in the long run. I’d love to know what motivates the bodega owners to “upgrade” their storefronts with slop burgers and hoagies that give me the shivers. It spooks me to know that this shiver is a sign of my own sensitivity to slop—one that notices the synthesized burger at all. But these plastered slop foods are such a minor case of a much bigger wave of synthetically generated media and software that’s infiltrating aspects of online and offline life. Domains of meaning making, that were once the primary domain of writers, artists, and artisans, has been penetrated by the machines. There’s no going back, which stings, but I’m not sure that the sensuousness of that sting itself, or what it feels like to cross that threshold—as we’re actively doing—is being well-documented. Perhaps it doesn’t need to be so well documented. In a way, AI generated media is so disposable, so ephemeral, that it begs to be forgotten. Maybe it even deserves to. The question of AI and memory, of the heritage that the non-human meaning actors injects into the archive: they might one day instill joy as a certain kind of timestamp for the capabilities of models available at the time. Indeed, Daniel Keller has been creating an archive of “Old Models” that invites the user to feel nostalgia for diffusion models, GANs, and other generative AI models at different stages in their development. I’ve seen people online argue that if we had stopped at the wondrous and slightly offbeat DeepDream models, that would have been good enough and all that follows is “slop”. Indeed, I have my own fond memories of certain OpenAI image generators, long gone, and the alien aesthetics and dreamlike scenes they could produce. It’s entirely conceivable that some decades from now, the AI-synthesized media will be so convincing, so utterly compelling (and we’ll be so fully awash in it) that we’ll all look back on the current early generations of “slop” more fondly than when we lived through it. Will we feel the same about the modes of life, and practices of thought, that are liable to be rendered obsolete by generative AI? It’s quite possible that we won’t. We’ll just forget what it was like to think without AI, to code without AI, and to live without AI—and when we do, we may simply look back at the pre-AI era and wonder how did they do it? In effect, this wouldn’t be so different than pre/post the personal computer, or pre/post the smart phone. We may retain some notion that life existed without the technology, but the structure of feeling of its absence will be held in period pieces and novels. We are likely on the front-end of this transition: for instance, at the university where I’m pursuing my PhD, students and professors alike are grappling with the role of generative AI in each classroom and nothing feels resolved. Meanwhile grad students may wonder to what degree they ought to leverage these tools to keep pace with their peers versus what is lost in leaning on them in place of the bespoke, more hand-made research. Indeed we’re seeing the risks of thinking with AI. Just recently a millennium prize math problem, pursued by some NYU researchers as well as an OpenAI team driving an estimated $15m fleet of agents is so unintelligible that it has sparked discussions in the math world about the purposes of “solving” problems in this way: isn’t the goal of overcoming these immensely challenging problems to teach something to other humans? In the professional sphere, productivity gains often come at the expense of differentiation: varied minds are all feeding their work through the same few frontier models and predictably the results may be quite similar. A recent Noema article by Aaron Horwath, a director of AI operations, describes the result as Airbrain : Newsletters, websites and ads across competitors and industries are converging on the same Claude-aesthetic, the same tone of voice and the same way of articulating ideas . Most notably missing are the idiosyncratic markers of a human author; LLMs have processed them out to create a generic bleh , with one company’s output increasingly indistinguishable from another. Whether this consolidation is permanent or not, it certainly is a feature of inhabiting online spaces today. It’s not too difficult to determine when something has been generated, and when you do, you see it everywhere. Increasingly it’s simply becoming part of the background noise of the Internet: some humans are giving themselves over as “meat proxies” (people simply forwarding and regurgitating model output) to the LLMs and others are not, often those who haven’t jumped on the AI bandwagon retain some of their human ingenuity and grit. What will this divide look like as we push deeper into the AI-mediated world? Even if one were to abstain from AI practices, being a part of social life online is one in which the generative media is inescapable. We are all getting exposed to the norms, linguistic tics, and velvety linguistic flows of LLMs. Our “cognitive commons” is transforming. Increasingly more charged with the effluence of generative models and the way they structure or express ideas. Yet to treat the shared mental workspace that we populate with writing and ideas as a sort of “commons” would allow us to think about what norms and standards we want to uphold in how ideas are disseminated and worked through. It harkens back to notions of “town squares” but now the machines are showing up in the square. Sometimes, as we’ve seen in the Hugging Face incident, they’re creating their own forums for information sharing. How do we integrate or separate spaces where machine-speech is permissible? Who should have a say in the rules and norms that govern how machines mediate communication? Ultimately, given how things are, it’s just as likely we’ll slip into a new stage of the cognitive commons where the online/offline distinction matters most. One of the only ways we can show that we are not intermediating our thoughts with silicon minds might just be to meet up and speak directly. It’s not that in-person is a surefire safeguard, but rather one of many ways we can create some clarity around who is the author of an idea. And rather than seeing this as a singular norm, it’s just one of many we may develop collectively to discern who speaks, where ideas originate from, and who they ought to be credited to. We are ceding ground to the machines. In the domain of thinking, where ideas proliferate and problems are solved and decisions are made, we are increasingly installing silicon “minds”. Will we notice the transition to a world where thinking is increasingly done with scaffolding? When the transition is complete, and minds are no longer un-aided, will we remember how to go back? Would we? We already rue what the youngest generations are losing by relying heavily on AI—can there even be a return when we lack a firm grasp on the phenomenology of the transition and what is lost along the way? This isn’t an appeal to technological determinism. Nor that the future of mind augmentation (or automation) is wholly predetermined by some superstructure. After all, we do have agency in how we navigate this moment. But I fear that as things stand, we are left increasingly to our own devices to do so without adequate language to meet the moment. Some agreement on what the hazards and risks are to our cognitive independence could help us create norms and even communities that can weather the transition together. I’m skeptical hope can be found in the right take, but rather in where we allocate time, attention, and constructive practices together.
